title: High Blood Pressure (Hypertension): Ayurvedic Causes, Diet & Daily Routine
excerpt: High blood pressure is called a “silent killer” because it often has no symptoms, yet it can slowly damage the heart, brain and kidneys. Learn the causes from an Ayurvedic view, how to check BP correctly, salt and diet, daily routine, yoga-pranayama, safe home remedies and when you must go to hospital immediately.
content:
High blood pressure (hypertension) is very common in India. According to the ICMR-INDIAB study (2023), about one in every three adults in the country has high BP, and many of them do not even know it. There are often no symptoms, which is why it is called the “silent killer”.

The good news is that with regular check-ups, less salt, the right diet, exercise, stress control and medicines when needed, BP can be kept well under control. This article is for information only — take treatment only on the advice of your Vaidya or doctor.

What is high blood pressure?

With every beat, the heart pushes blood into the arteries. The pressure of blood on the walls of the arteries is the blood pressure. It is written as two numbers — for example 120/80 mmHg. The upper number (systolic) is the pressure during a heartbeat and the lower number (diastolic) is the pressure between two beats.

When BP measured correctly on different days repeatedly comes to 140/90 mmHg or more, it is considered high blood pressure. Below 120/80 is considered normal, and people with 130–139/80–89 also need lifestyle changes and regular check-ups. BP that stays high for a long time increases the risk of heart attack, stroke (paralysis), kidney disease and eye problems.

The Ayurvedic view

The ancient Ayurvedic texts have no separate disease named “blood pressure”, because there was no instrument to measure BP at that time. But its causes and effects are understood in terms of Vyana Vayu (which circulates blood throughout the body), Rakta dhatu and the heart (Hridaya). Excess salt, spicy and fried food and anger vitiate Pitta and Rakta; heavy food, laziness and obesity increase Kapha and Meda and cause obstruction in the srotas (channels/arteries); and worry, little sleep and hurry increase Vata.

The first aim of Ayurveda is to protect health before disease occurs, which is most useful in lifestyle-related problems like high BP. Charaka Samhita describes the purpose of Ayurveda as follows:

प्रयोजनं चास्य स्वस्थस्य स्वास्थ्यरक्षणमातुरस्य विकारप्रशमनं च ।
— Charaka Samhita, Sutra Sthana 30

Meaning: The purpose of Ayurveda is to protect the health of the healthy and to relieve the disease of the sick. That is why diet, daily routine and peace of mind are the foundation of high BP care.

Main causes and risks

  • Too much salt in food — pickles, papad, namkeen, chips, sauces, packaged and outside food
  • Excess weight, especially belly fat
  • Lack of exercise and sitting most of the time
  • Stress, anger, worry and less than 6 hours of sleep daily
  • Smoking, tobacco and alcohol
  • Increasing age and someone in the family having high BP
  • Diabetes, kidney disease, thyroid problems, or breathing pauses during sleep with snoring (sleep apnoea)
  • Some medicines, such as long-term painkillers or steroids

Symptoms

Most people with high BP have no symptoms — so “I don't feel anything” does not mean BP is fine. Some people may have these problems:

  • Heaviness or pain in the back of the head, especially in the morning
  • Dizziness or tiredness
  • Feeling a fast heartbeat, restlessness
  • Poor sleep, irritability
  • Sometimes nosebleeds or blurred vision

Checking BP correctly

After the age of 30, everyone should get their BP checked at least once a year. When measuring at home with a digital machine:

  • Do not have tea or coffee, smoke or exercise for 30 minutes before; empty your bladder first
  • Sit quietly on a chair for 5 minutes, back supported, feet on the floor, without talking
  • Keep the arm on a table at heart level; tie the cuff on the bare arm
  • Measure twice, 1 minute apart, and write down both readings

As needed, the doctor may also advise blood sugar, cholesterol, kidney test (creatinine), urine test and ECG.

Diet: what to eat, what to avoid

Diet is the biggest weapon in controlling BP. According to WHO, an adult should take less than 5 grams (about one small teaspoon) of salt in the whole day — this includes the salt already present in food.

What to eat

  • Vegetables: bottle gourd, ridge gourd, pointed gourd (parwal), pumpkin, spinach, fenugreek leaves, carrot, beetroot — plenty in every meal
  • Fruits: banana, pomegranate, papaya, guava, apple, orange, amla
  • Grains: barley, oats, bajra, jowar, daliya, whole-wheat roti
  • Pulses: moong, masoor, chana — with little salt and little oil
  • Milk-buttermilk: low-fat milk, thin buttermilk without salt
  • Seeds-nuts: flaxseed, a few unsalted almonds and walnuts
  • For taste, use lemon, cumin, coriander, mint, garlic and ginger instead of salt

What to avoid or greatly reduce

  • Pickles, papad, namkeen, chips, bhujia, sauces, instant noodles
  • Sprinkling extra salt on top and chaat masala on salads and fruits
  • Fried food, dalda/vanaspati, bakery items and fast food
  • Sweets, too much sugar and cold drinks
  • Too much tea-coffee and energy drinks
  • Alcohol, cigarettes, bidis, gutkha and tobacco

Daily routine, yoga and pranayama

  • Walk briskly for at least 30 minutes daily (5 or more days a week)
  • If overweight, reduce weight gradually — even a little weight loss lowers BP
  • Sleep on time at night and get 7–8 hours of sleep
  • Calm the mind daily with 10–15 minutes of meditation, japa or prayer
  • Avoid anger, hurry, and mobile/TV late at night
  • Take medicines at the same time every day and keep a BP diary

Yoga and pranayama

  • Asanas: Shavasana, Makarasana, Balasana, Vajrasana, Tadasana, slow breathing while sitting in Sukhasana
  • Pranayama: Anulom-Vilom, Bhramari, Sheetali (slowly and without force)

In high BP, do not do Kapalbhati, Bhastrika, long breath-holding (kumbhaka) or inverted poses like Shirshasana and Sarvangasana. Ask your doctor before heavy weight-lifting exercises. If BP is above 180/110, first get BP under control, then start exercise. Learn yoga only from a trained teacher.

Safe home remedies

  • Garlic: regular use of garlic in food
  • Amla: fresh amla or amla juice (diluted with water)
  • Bottle gourd (lauki): lauki vegetable or fresh juice — if the juice tastes bitter, do not drink it at all
  • Coconut water and banana: rich in potassium
  • Fenugreek and flaxseed: in small amounts in food

People with kidney disease must ask their doctor before taking coconut water, bananas and potassium-containing salt (low-sodium salt), because a rise in potassium can be dangerous for them. People on blood-thinning medicines should ask their doctor before taking extra garlic. Home remedies are not a substitute for medicines.

Ayurvedic herbs — with caution

Ayurveda mentions several medicines for the heart and mind, such as Arjuna (bark), Sarpagandha, Brahmi, Jatamansi, Ashwagandha, Punarnava and Rasona (garlic). However:

  • Which medicine, in what dose and for how long — the Vaidya decides this only after looking at each person's prakriti, pulse, age, BP readings and current medicines.
  • Sarpagandha is a strong medicine — never take it on your own; it can be harmful in depression, stomach ulcers and pregnancy.
  • Never stop or reduce your ongoing BP medicine on your own. Taking herbs along with medicines can make BP fall too low, so check BP more often when starting any new medicine. Liquorice (mulethi) can raise BP — avoid it in high BP.
  • In pregnancy, breastfeeding, children and the elderly, give any medicine only on the advice of a Vaidya/doctor. Beware of claims like “BP cured forever” or “we will stop all your medicines”.

When to go to hospital immediately

  • BP of 180/120 or more along with chest pain, breathlessness or a very severe headache
  • One side of the face drooping, weakness or numbness in one arm or leg, difficulty speaking — this may be a stroke (paralysis); every minute counts
  • Sudden blurred vision, confusion, fainting or a seizure
  • Rising BP in pregnancy, with headache, blurred vision or sudden swelling of hands, feet or face
  • BP very low on repeated measurement (for example below 90/60) with dizziness or weakness

Summary — points to remember

  • BP check every year after 30 — even without symptoms
  • Less than one small teaspoon of salt in the whole day; stop pickles, papad and namkeen
  • Daily 30-minute walk, weight control, good sleep and peace of mind
  • Completely give up smoking, tobacco and alcohol
  • Do not stop medicines on your own; Ayurvedic treatment only on the advice of an experienced Vaidya
